name: Ross Mountjoy
summary: Self-taught full-stack developer with over ten years of experience building and scaling web applications, from system architecture and backend APIs through frontend UI and the infrastructure underneath. The last few years have gone deep on AI integration: building against the Anthropic and OpenAI APIs, writing Claude Code extensions and MCP servers, wiring agents into real services through OpenAPI specs, and running local models with Ollama for private inference. Came into the field through personal projects and open source, including Home Assistant and DashMachine, which has passed 11 million Docker Hub pulls.

highlights: Stayed on as an independent contractor after four years as a full-time employee; Savi is now the main client of Mountjoy Software Solutions.
Owns the AWS infrastructure and runs their SAML single sign-on service.
AI engineering, including LLM integration and agent tooling.
Migrated their entire stack off EC2 and onto ECS, containerising a legacy PHP application and modernising the stack around it.
Built a custom SAML identity provider and service provider platform to run single sign-on for their users.
Replaced the DocuSign integration in the core application flow with an in-house PDF generation, signature and faxing system.
Wrote their Bitbucket Pipelines CI/CD, which builds and deploys the containerised stack.
Stood up Qdrant and built semantic search over the help centre articles behind the Savi Assistant, using embeddings and cosine similarity retrieval.
Full-stack development across a PHP, Laravel, Python and React codebase.
Owned the AWS infrastructure, including ECS, ALB, IAM, Cognito, S3 and Route 53.
Sole developer of the web application for a startup turning over $30m+ a year, which was sold to Revive, Inc.
Built and ran the Python, FastAPI and Vue.js codebase end to end.
Served buyers and sellers across the DC Metro area.
Specialised in the business side of the job: graphic design, business systems, online marketing, Google Ads and SEO.
Consulted for other agents in the area on the same things, which is where the software career started.

projects.name: Savi Assistant
projects.blurb: Client-facing AI assistant for Savi. Retrieval over the help centre, streamed replies, and tool calling.
projects.details: Built for Savi as their main client-facing assistant. Help centre content is chunked out of PDFs, embedded, and indexed in a vector database, so answers are retrieved by meaning rather than keyword match. Replies stream to the browser over Server-Sent Events, and the model can call tools to act rather than only answer. Built on the Laravel AI SDK against the Anthropic API. The retrieval approach is the same cosine-similarity technique behind Gem's memory system, pointed at a different corpus.

projects.name: Gem
projects.blurb: Fully self-hosted household AI assistant. Three repos, a dual-GPU box in the house, one Flutter codebase across Android, iOS, iPad and web, and a memory system that metabolises conversations while nobody is looking.
projects.details:
Gem is the assistant my household actually uses. Nothing about her is a demo: she runs on a machine in my house, answers on a phone, a browser and an iPad mounted in the kitchen, and the people talking to her are my family. Three repositories — a FastAPI server, a Flutter client, and an infrastructure and operations repo for the box she runs on.

**The hardware and why there are two of everything.** She runs on a dual-GPU Ubuntu box: an AMD Radeon AI PRO R9700 with 32GB for the large conversation model, and an NVIDIA RTX 3060 with 12GB for embeddings, speech and the small utility model. A single Ollama process cannot split one model across mixed AMD and NVIDIA silicon, so each card runs its own Ollama instance in Docker and a model string can name the instance that should serve it. ROCm runs in a container rather than on the host because the box is on a newer Ubuntu than ROCm's support matrix covers; the container brings its own userspace and only needs the kernel driver.

**Routing, and deleting the classifier.** A small model used to sit in front of every message deciding whether a tool was needed and how hard to think. It was a telephone game: the small model's limits had to be compensated for with an ever more rigid keyword-driven prompt, and tools fired on sentences that merely mentioned a trigger word — "we've been adding things to the shopping list" would fire a memory write. I deleted it. The 31B conversation model now makes that call itself, natively, in the same pass it uses to answer: tools are attached for exactly one round against its real prompt, and if it calls one the tool runs and the model streams a second time with no tools attached. That guarantees a tool can fire at most once per message, which matters because a second tools-attached round produced real duplicate side effects — two identical reminders for one request, because a model does not reliably recognise its own completed action as done rather than repeatable.

**Memory is a background process, not something that happens mid-sentence.** Nothing writes to memory during a conversation. Ten minutes after the last WebSocket in the house closes, a loop inside the API process distils what is new in each conversation into atomic notes, and on a longer cadence audits the whole store: kill duplicates, apply a "so what?" test, split summary-shaped notes, and resolve contradictions by betting on the recent version rather than keeping both. It freezes the instant anyone reconnects, cancelling the in-flight model call so the GPU is free before the person's message arrives, and every tool execution is shielded so a freeze lands between turns and cannot tear a note's three stores apart mid-write.

This replaced a 3am cron job, and the reason was a real failure. Every live memory write went through a merge prompt instructed to preserve every existing detail and never remove anything — which is precisely why notes could only grow. A correction landed as an addition, so the store accumulated contradictions instead of settling. The loop replaces content instead of appending to it.

**Retrieval is two-stage, and the second stage is the interesting one.** Notes live in three places kept in sync by one module: a flat markdown vault, MySQL rows for ownership and tags, and a Qdrant point for the embedding. Rather than folders, a note is owned by one or more people and carries tags — ownership is the entire access check, so a note you do not own is indistinguishable from one that does not exist. On a query, the question is embedded once, and that same vector is matched against a separate Qdrant collection of tag-name embeddings; tags that clear a threshold become a hard payload filter before cosine similarity runs inside the narrowed subset. Tag selection therefore costs no extra model round-trip — it is one more cosine lookup against a tiny collection.

The tag threshold sits deliberately far above the note threshold, because the two failures are not symmetric: a weak note match costs some noise in the prompt, but a weak tag match filters genuinely relevant notes out of the search entirely. So narrowing is only ever allowed to reduce noise — if the tag stage matches nothing confidently the search is ownership-only, and if a narrowed search comes back empty it is retried without the tags. Only topic tags are embedded; the structural ones a person never says out loud would add vocabulary that can only mis-match.

**Every answer leaves a forensic trace.** One JSON blob per message records the retrieval query with every Qdrant hit and score including the near-misses that did not clear the threshold, the whole tag pre-filter and whether the fallback fired, each tool's raw arguments and result, and the exact final message list sent to the model. Debugging "why did she answer that" is a query, not a guess — and a note that never reached the similarity search at all would otherwise be invisible.

**Who is talking.** The kitchen iPad is shared, so "what's on my list" has to know whose list. A CPU-only service wraps SpeechBrain's ECAPA-TDNN speaker embeddings; a person reads four phrases once and from then on each sentence is matched against their centroid by cosine, needing to clear both an absolute threshold and a margin ahead of the runner-up. Only the embedding is stored, never the audio. On a confident match the transcribe endpoint returns a 30-minute token for that person, so the prompt, the retrieval and every tool are already scoped correctly without the chat endpoint knowing anything about voices. An unsure match is a real guest account with nothing in it, because before that the fallback was the iPad's own login — and a stranger asking for "my list" got mine.

**Wake word.** "Hey Gem" is detected on-device by an ONNX classifier I trained on the box from recordings of the household, running over a rolling two-second audio ring ten times a second. It replaced Apple's on-device speech recogniser plus a regex of near-misses, which peaked around six wakes in ten and was markedly worse for my wife than for me: a dictation engine has no idea "Gem" is a word, returns text rather than confidence, and closes its request on the very silence that precedes someone saying it.

**Speech, and the name problem.** Whisper handles transcription at int8, which halved its VRAM against float16 with no measurable accuracy loss once a cleanup pass runs. That pass is not optional: Whisper hears "Jem" for "Gem" every single time. A utility model strips fillers and fixes mis-hearings, and because the model does not always act on the name, a deterministic pass runs after it — her name following a greeting becomes Gem, while "my friend Jim" is left alone. Kokoro does text to speech locally, so no audio leaves the house.

**What she can actually do.** Web search, weather, timers, reminders and recurring tasks, shared lists, notes, a news feed whose search queries she picks herself from what she knows about each person, read-only calendar sync from subscribed ICS feeds, Plaid transaction sync, and Spotify — the box is the house's speaker over Bluetooth, with a level meter feeding the console's visualiser over UDP. The client surfaces most of these as docked mini apps inside the chat rather than separate screens, plus Android home-screen widgets drawn as bitmaps through a dot-matrix font because RemoteViews cannot host Flutter.

**The console.** The iPad on the kitchen counter is the same Flutter codebase in a different mode: an ambient face with weather, the day's agenda and a voice visualiser. It sleeps after a minute of quiet and wakes on the wake word, a touch, or motion — motion from the front camera reduced to a 24×18 brightness grid at 4fps, with no frame kept, and the camera armed only while she is asleep so it is never on while someone is talking to her. It connects as a passive socket: it gets every event but is left out of the presence count, because an iPad switched on all day with nobody at it otherwise froze the memory loop indefinitely. The loop shows its work on the glass — a distinct face for housekeeping, so nobody mistakes it for an answer on its way.

**Where it is now.** In daily use by my household. The client ships to real devices through Firebase App Distribution. Memory, retrieval, voice identity, the wake word, the mini apps and the music hub are all live; proactive communication is the next thing, and the hooks for it — the notable items each cycle collects, per-note provenance back to the conversation that produced it — are already in place. The honest gap is that retrieval is dense vectors plus a payload filter, not hybrid search in the strict sense: there is no lexical ranking anywhere, which is why keyword search over memories is a substring scan. Adding a sparse BM25 vector and fusing with reciprocal rank fusion is the documented fix, and it needs a collection rebuild because named vectors can only be configured at creation.

media.caption: The kitchen console. Ambient weather, the day's agenda and a voice visualiser; it sleeps after a minute and wakes on "hey Gem", a touch, or motion.
Memories: the notes the idle loop wrote from conversations, tagged and vector-indexed. A person can edit one but never creates one.
Notes are the other half of the same tables: a person's own scratchpad, never embedded and invisible to the audit, so Gem cannot silently rewrite one.
Web search. The conversation model decides for itself that a question is time-sensitive enough to need it, then answers from what came back.
Weather, from a free geocoding and forecast API. The location argument is optional and falls back to a household setting when the model leaves it out.
Shared lists, docked as a mini app inside the chat rather than a separate screen.
Calendar. Events sync read-only from subscribed ICS feeds, so they are editable at the source and nowhere else.

projects.name: Pip
projects.blurb: The predecessor to Gem. An OpenAI-backed assistant living on a Raspberry Pi with a 3 inch display, in a 3D-printed case mounted on the kitchen wall.
projects.details:
Pip was the first attempt at the idea Gem now does properly: a household assistant that is a physical object rather than an app. A Raspberry Pi behind a 3 inch display, in a case designed and printed for it, bolted to the kitchen wall with a camera and a shotgun microphone above it. Idle, it showed a pair of eyes with the temperature and time; spoken to, it answered through the OpenAI API.

Two repositories: a Python backend and a separate frontend for the display. Everything Gem got right about being local and owned came out of what Pip got wrong by depending on somebody else's API.

media.caption: Mounted on the kitchen wall, camera and microphone above the display.
The display on the bench during the build, showing the idle eyes, temperature and time.

projects.name: DashMachine
projects.blurb: Self-hosted application dashboard and bookmark manager. 1,265 GitHub stars and 11.3 million Docker Hub pulls.
projects.details: An open source dashboard for self-hosters, written in Python and Flask. The reach is the interesting part: 11.3 million pulls of the official image on Docker Hub, 1,265 GitHub stars and 121 forks. That meant supporting a large user base across wildly varied deployments, reviewing outside contributions, and keeping the container small enough to be trivial to run.

projects.name: VectorCloud
projects.blurb: Web dashboard for the Anki Vector robot, officially adopted by Anki.
projects.details: A self-hosted web interface and control surface for the Anki Vector robot, built on Vector's SDK. Anki officially adopted it, which is the part worth noting: an open source side project picked up by the hardware manufacturer whose product it extended. 124 GitHub stars and 19 forks.

projects.name: This site
projects.blurb: Flutter web on S3 and CloudFront, FastAPI on ECS Fargate, all defined in CDK and shipped by GitHub Actions. The assistant you are talking to runs on Bedrock embeddings and a Qdrant collection of this record.
projects.details:
The diagram below is the whole thing. One CloudFront distribution fronts two origins: the default behaviour serves the Flutter bundle out of a private S3 bucket over Origin Access Control, and /api/* goes to an Application Load Balancer in front of a FastAPI task on ECS Fargate. Because both live behind the same distribution the browser is same-origin with the API, so there is no CORS anywhere. The load balancer's security group admits only CloudFront's origin-facing prefix list, which means api.mountjoy.io cannot be reached directly even though it has a public certificate.

The VPC has no NAT gateway. Tasks sit in public subnets with a public IP and reach S3 and DynamoDB over gateway endpoints, which costs nothing, rather than paying for a managed NAT to do the same work.

All of it is AWS CDK in Python, split into four stacks so the stateful pieces can carry termination protection and RETAIN policies while the compute and edge stacks stay disposable. GitHub Actions deploys on every push to main through OIDC federation, so there are no AWS keys stored anywhere in the repo or in GitHub. DynamoDB is a single table holding rate-limit counters keyed by a salted hash of the caller's IP, with a TTL so old rows expire themselves.

The assistant is Claude with a system prompt built from this same profile record. Portfolio content is embedded with Amazon Bedrock Titan and indexed in Qdrant, which both retrieves context for answers and drives the interactive graph you get from /projects. The system prompt is assembled once at import so the cached prefix stays byte-identical between requests and prompt caching actually hits; retrieved excerpts go into the user turn instead, where they cannot break the cache.

Source is public.

media.caption: Production architecture. One CloudFront distribution fronts both the S3 bundle and the Fargate API, so the browser is same-origin with the API. The load balancer only admits the CloudFront prefix list.
